title: Except anger and pride
hookLine: for anger and pride he says go far toward the opposite
last: THE MIDDLE PATH IS THE WAY OF THE LORD.

cards: "Now the man Moses was very meek." That's a line from the book of Numbers. Maimonides lingers on one word in it.
Not meek. Very meek. In his code he teaches that good traits live in the middle, between two extremes.

Then, a little further on, he stops and makes an exception. There are a couple of traits, he says, where the middle is still too close to danger. For these, a person should go far, all the way toward the opposite end.

teach.h: PRIDE: NOT A LITTLE HUMBLE. VERY.
teach.b: Except anger and pride. Take pride first. With most traits, Maimonides says, aim for the middle.
But not here. It isn't enough to be a little humble. A person should be very humble, lowly of spirit, like Moses.
That's why the verse says very meek. And he points to the sages in Pirkei Avot, who said it twice over: be very, very humble. Pride, for Maimonides, isn't a trait you can safely keep a little of.

teach.h: ANGER: GO FAR TO THE OTHER SIDE.
teach.b: Anger, he says, is a very bad trait, and here too a person should go far to the other side, training themselves not to get angry even over something that seems to deserve it.
He passes on a hard saying of the sages: getting angry is like worshiping idols. In the moment of rage, something else sits on the throne. Then, a practical twist.
Sometimes a parent or a leader needs others to take a matter seriously. Maimonides allows them to show anger on the outside, while staying calm within.
The face may be stern. The heart stays still. Now step back and look at why these two are the exceptions.

teach.h: BOTH PUT THE SELF AT THE CENTER.
teach.b: Pride and anger both put the self at the center of the room. Most traits can be balanced. These two, he seems to say, tip over too easily, so he keeps them far from the edge.

how: Students of Jewish ethics study Maimonides' Laws of Character Traits, chapter 2, where he names anger and pride as the exceptions to the middle path.

games.q: what does “except anger and pride” mean?
o: two traits to steer far from, not just to balance
two feelings that are sinful just to have
two traits a good leader needs in moderate doses

games.q: except anger and pride — tap the pairs.
p: a parent who must be stern

s: Maimonides says a little pride is healthy, in the middle
pride is an exception: he says to be very humble, like Moses.
he passes on a saying that anger is like worshiping idols
the sages compared getting angry to idol worship.
a parent or leader may show anger outwardly, while staying calm inside.

games.q: you're a parent, and your child needs to know something matters. you're Maimonides. what do you do?
o: lose your temper, so they remember.
look stern on the outside, and stay calm inside.
games.why: he allows a stern face for the sake of teaching, but the heart should stay calm.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you need to be right, or seen, or first, and notice what the body says: a lift in the chest, a tight jaw.
Then, gently, let it come down one step, not crushed, just lowered, like setting a heavy bag on the floor.

wordCard.voice: Except anger and pride. The two traits where Maimonides says to leave the middle and go far toward the opposite: very humble, and very slow to anger. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: humility, the trait Numbers gives Moses: he was very humble, anav.

carryVoice: Your line: far from pride. And far from anger, too, even when it seems deserved. See you tomorrow.
